blocks.en: The Olivet Discourse and Three Questions
blocks.es_reference: El Discurso del Monte de los Olivos y Tres Preguntas

blocks.en: The burning question about the end of the age has been argued for two thousand years. We all want to know what happens next, and the disciples felt the same. As Jesus and the disciples were leaving the temple, He said that not one stone would be left upon another. On the Mount of Olives they came with three questions (Matthew 24:3): when will the temple be destroyed, what will be the sign of Your coming, and what is the sign of the end of the age? Jesus answered all three, but the answers are woven together so tightly that interpreters still debate which verse belongs to which question. This is the great discourse on the last things, and we should hold it with humility, for it was given less to satisfy our curiosity than to make us ready.
blocks.es_reference: La pregunta candente sobre el fin de la era se ha discutido durante dos mil años. Todos queremos saber qué sucederá después, y los discípulos sentían lo mismo. Mientras Jesús y los discípulos salían del templo, Él dijo que no quedaría piedra sobre piedra. En el Monte de los Olivos vinieron con tres preguntas (Mateo 24:3): ¿cuándo será destruido el templo?, ¿cuál será la señal de tu venida?, y ¿cuál es la señal del fin de la era? Jesús respondió a las tres, pero las respuestas están entretejidas tan estrechamente que los intérpretes aún debaten qué versículo corresponde a cada pregunta. Este es el gran discurso sobre las cosas finales, y debemos sostenerlo con humildad, porque fue dado menos para satisfacer nuestra curiosidad que para prepararnos.

blocks.en: The temple fell in A.D. 70, about forty years after Jesus' prediction, so that part of His answer was fulfilled within a single generation. The Roman legions under Titus surrounded the city and cut every supply line. Inside the walls the people were destroyed by famine, by civil war between rival factions, and by disease. The historian Josephus records starvation so severe that people ate the leather of their shoes and even, in one tragic case, turned to cannibalism. The Second Temple, the heart of Jewish identity, was burned to its foundations; the gold ornaments melted, and soldiers pried apart the very stones to recover it, literally fulfilling the word that not one stone would be left upon another. Hundreds of thousands perished, and tens of thousands were carried off as prisoners, sent to the mines, sold as slaves, or forced to fight as gladiators. For the first-century Jew this was the absolute end of the world as he knew it: the priesthood ceased, the sacrifices ended, and the central place of worship was gone. Today only a portion of the western retaining wall remains, where Jews still come to pray and to place written petitions in the cracks of the stone.
blocks.es_reference: El templo cayó en el año 70 d.C., unos cuarenta años después de la predicción de Jesús, de modo que esa parte de su respuesta se cumplió dentro de una sola generación. Las legiones romanas dirigidas por Tito rodearon la ciudad y cortaron toda línea de suministro. Dentro de las murallas la gente fue destruida por el hambre, por la guerra civil entre facciones rivales, y por la enfermedad. El historiador Josefo registra una inanición tan severa que la gente comía el cuero de sus zapatos y, en un caso trágico, recurrió al canibalismo. El Segundo Templo, corazón de la identidad judía, fue quemado hasta sus cimientos; los ornamentos de oro se derritieron, y los soldados separaron las piedras mismas para recuperarlo, cumpliendo literalmente la palabra de que no quedaría piedra sobre piedra. Cientos de miles perecieron, y decenas de miles fueron llevados como prisioneros, enviados a las minas, vendidos como esclavos, u obligados a luchar como gladiadores. Para el judío del primer siglo este fue el fin absoluto del mundo tal como lo conocía: el sacerdocio cesó, los sacrificios terminaron, y el lugar central de adoración desapareció. Hoy solo queda una porción del muro de contención occidental, donde los judíos todavía vienen a orar y a colocar peticiones escritas en las grietas de la piedra.

blocks.en: Before that fall and stretching on toward His final coming, Jesus described the character of the whole age. There would be false christs who deceive many, wars and rumors of wars, famines and earthquakes — but these are only the beginning of sorrows, not the end itself. His people would be hated and persecuted, yet "this gospel of the kingdom will be preached in all the world as a witness to all the nations, and then the end will come" (Matthew 24:14). He spoke of the abomination of desolation and a great tribulation, and finally of the Son of Man coming on the clouds of heaven with power and great glory, gathering His elect. Interpreters differ over how much of this language pointed to A.D. 70 and how much reaches forward to the final coming, and faithful readers hold different views. What is certain is the lesson of the fig tree: when these things begin, the end is near, and "heaven and earth will pass away, but My words will by no means pass away" (Matthew 24:35).
blocks.es_reference: Antes de esa caída y extendiéndose hacia su venida final, Jesús describió el carácter de toda la era. Habría falsos cristos que engañan a muchos, guerras y rumores de guerras, hambres y terremotos — pero esto es solo el principio de dolores, no el fin mismo. Su pueblo sería aborrecido y perseguido, y sin embargo "será predicado este evangelio del reino en todo el mundo, para testimonio a todas las naciones; y entonces vendrá el fin" (Mateo 24:14). Habló de la abominación desoladora y de una gran tribulación, y por fin del Hijo del Hombre viniendo sobre las nubes del cielo con poder y gran gloria, reuniendo a sus escogidos. Los intérpretes difieren sobre cuánto de este lenguaje apuntaba al año 70 y cuánto alcanza hacia la venida final, y lectores fieles sostienen distintas opiniones. Lo cierto es la lección de la higuera: cuando estas cosas comiencen, el fin está cerca, y "el cielo y la tierra pasarán, mas mis palabras no pasarán" (Mateo 24:35).

blocks.en: When Is the End? No One Knows
blocks.es_reference: ¿Cuándo Es el Fin? Nadie lo Sabe

blocks.en: About the date of His return Jesus said plainly that not even He knew it, but the Father only (Matthew 24:36). That has not stopped people from making predictions for two thousand years, and every one of them has been wrong — every single one. By the Old Testament standard of Deuteronomy 18, a prophet whose prediction fails is a false prophet, so by Scripture's own test these date-setters disqualified themselves. The 2011 prediction of Harold Camping is a modern warning: using an elaborate, homemade numerology to get around the Bible's caution, he convinced thousands that May 21, 2011, would be the day. When nothing happened, he simply moved the date to October. The harm was real and lasting — people drained their retirement savings, abandoned their careers, and suffered deep spiritual disillusionment when the predicted day came and went. Claiming divine authority for a human calculation does not only fail; it wounds the people who trusted it.
blocks.es_reference: Sobre la fecha de su regreso Jesús dijo claramente que ni siquiera Él la sabía, sino solo el Padre (Mateo 24:36). Eso no ha impedido que la gente haga predicciones durante dos mil años, y todas han estado equivocadas — todas y cada una. Según el estándar del Antiguo Testamento de Deuteronomio 18, un profeta cuya predicción falla es un falso profeta, así que por la propia prueba de la Escritura estos fijadores de fechas se descalificaron a sí mismos. La predicción de Harold Camping en 2011 es una advertencia moderna: usando una numerología elaborada y casera para eludir la cautela de la Biblia, convenció a miles de que el 21 de mayo de 2011 sería el día. Cuando nada sucedió, simplemente cambió la fecha a octubre. El daño fue real y duradero — la gente agotó sus ahorros de jubilación, abandonó sus carreras, y sufrió profunda desilusión espiritual cuando el día predicho pasó. Afirmar autoridad divina para un cálculo humano no solo fracasa; hiere a los que confiaron en él.

blocks.en: Christians who love the very same Bible have long held different views about the thousand years of Revelation 20 and the sequence of end-time events. The premillennial view holds that Christ returns before a coming reign on the earth; the amillennial view understands the thousand years as a picture of Christ's present reign between His two comings; and the postmillennial view expects Christ to return after a long age in which the gospel's influence grows. Sincere, Bible-loving believers have held each of these for centuries, and none of these positions has ever been a test of Christian fellowship. On the central things every view agrees: Jesus Christ will return bodily and visibly, the dead will be raised, and there will be a final judgment. Rather than dividing over the order of events, we do better to stand together on what is certain and to be ready.
blocks.es_reference: Los cristianos que aman la misma Biblia han sostenido por mucho tiempo distintas opiniones sobre los mil años de Apocalipsis 20 y la secuencia de los eventos del fin. La posición premilenial sostiene que Cristo vuelve antes de un reinado venidero sobre la tierra; la posición amilenial entiende los mil años como un cuadro del reinado presente de Cristo entre sus dos venidas; y la posición posmilenial espera que Cristo vuelva después de una larga era en que crece la influencia del evangelio. Creyentes sinceros y amantes de la Biblia han sostenido cada una de estas por siglos, y ninguna de estas posiciones ha sido jamás una prueba de compañerismo cristiano. En las cosas centrales toda opinión concuerda: Jesucristo volverá corporal y visiblemente, los muertos serán resucitados, y habrá un juicio final. En vez de dividirnos por el orden de los eventos, hacemos mejor en mantenernos juntos en lo que es cierto y en estar preparados.

blocks.en: What Will Happen on That Day

The first time Jesus came, He came as the suffering Servant of Isaiah — born in a stable, rejected by His own, crucified between two thieves. When He comes again, He will come as a conquering King. The contrast could not be more complete. First Thessalonians 4 gives the clearest picture of that day: the dead in Christ will rise first, then those who are alive will be caught up to join them, all at the sound of the trumpet. The believers in Thessalonica were anxious about loved ones who had died while waiting for that return, and Paul assured them that death is no barrier — those who have died in Christ will not be left behind but will be the first to rise. Scripture also rejects the idea of "soul sleep": the Lord told the thief he would be with Him in Paradise that very day, and Paul says that to be absent from the body is to be present with the Lord. The "sleep" the Bible speaks of is the rest of the body in the grave, not the soul, which remains awake and with God. I remember riding to a cemetery with a funeral director in South Dakota who said proudly, "You know, the crypts we put in the ground last two hundred years" — and I asked him the obvious question: what happens after that? The body is only the mailbox. Once the letter is posted it is already in the sender's hands, and though the mailbox may rust and be replaced, the letter — the real person — is kept safe until the day it is delivered. The trumpet that announces that day carried rich meaning for Jewish ears, for the shofar sounded at Sinai when God came down, at the Jubilee when slaves went free, and at the crowning of kings — presence, liberation, and coronation all at once. C.S. Lewis observed that the second coming splits history into everything before it and everything after, so that this present age is only a kind of preface; we are not yet in the main story.
blocks.es_reference: La primera vez que Jesús vino, vino como el Siervo sufriente de Isaías — nacido en un establo, rechazado por los suyos, crucificado entre dos ladrones. Cuando venga otra vez, vendrá como un Rey conquistador. El contraste no podría ser más completo. Primera de Tesalonicenses 4 da el cuadro más claro de ese día: los muertos en Cristo resucitarán primero, luego los que estén vivos serán arrebatados para unirse a ellos, todo al sonido de la trompeta. Los creyentes en Tesalónica estaban ansiosos por los seres queridos que habían muerto mientras esperaban ese regreso, y Pablo les aseguró que la muerte no es barrera — los que han muerto en Cristo no serán dejados atrás sino que serán los primeros en resucitar. La Escritura también rechaza la idea del "sueño del alma": el Señor dijo al ladrón que estaría con Él en el Paraíso ese mismo día, y Pablo dice que estar ausente del cuerpo es estar presente con el Señor. El "sueño" del que habla la Biblia es el descanso del cuerpo en la tumba, no del alma, que permanece despierta y con Dios. Recuerdo que iba hacia un cementerio con un director de funeraria en Dakota del Sur que dijo con orgullo: "¿Sabe? Las criptas que ponemos en el suelo duran doscientos años" — y le hice la pregunta obvia: ¿qué sucede después? El cuerpo es solo el buzón. Una vez que la carta es enviada ya está en manos del remitente, y aunque el buzón se oxide y sea reemplazado, la carta — la persona real — se guarda a salvo hasta el día en que sea entregada. La trompeta que anuncia ese día llevaba un rico significado para el oído judío, porque el shofar sonaba en el Sinaí cuando Dios descendía, en el Jubileo cuando los esclavos quedaban libres, y en la coronación de los reyes — presencia, liberación y coronación a la vez. C.S. Lewis observó que la segunda venida divide la historia en todo lo anterior a ella y todo lo posterior, de modo que esta era presente es solo una especie de prefacio; todavía no estamos en la historia principal.

blocks.en: There will be astonishing changes when we meet the Lord. We will receive glorified bodies like His resurrection body. He passed through locked doors; He was recognized by His closest friends, and sometimes not, as on the road to Emmaus where two of them walked and talked with Him for miles before their eyes were opened; He ate fish on the shore, not because He had to but because He could; and in that same glorified body He was taken up until a cloud received Him out of sight. But something even greater than a glorified body awaits us. First John 3:2 says that when He appears we shall see Him as He is, and we shall be like Him. In the Old Testament no one could look directly upon God; Moses saw only His back, for the glory would have destroyed sinful men. But on that day we will see Him face to face, and I believe we will be able to bear it because we will have been made like Him. Somehow — and this is one of the great mysteries of Scripture — God will make us holy without erasing who we are. He will purify us without deleting us. Our identity, our memory, our freedom: all of it carried through a holiness we cannot yet imagine. How He will do this is a great mystery.
blocks.es_reference: Habrá cambios asombrosos cuando nos encontremos con el Señor. Recibiremos cuerpos glorificados como su cuerpo de resurrección. Él atravesó puertas cerradas; fue reconocido por sus amigos más cercanos, y a veces no, como en el camino a Emaús donde dos de ellos caminaron y hablaron con Él por kilómetros antes de que sus ojos fueran abiertos; comió pescado en la orilla, no porque tuviera que hacerlo sino porque podía; y en ese mismo cuerpo glorificado fue llevado arriba hasta que una nube lo recibió fuera de su vista. Pero algo aún más grande que un cuerpo glorificado nos espera. Primera de Juan 3:2 dice que cuando Él aparezca le veremos como Él es, y seremos semejantes a Él. En el Antiguo Testamento nadie podía mirar directamente a Dios; Moisés solo vio su espalda, porque la gloria habría destruido a los hombres pecadores. Pero en ese día le veremos cara a cara, y creo que podremos soportarlo porque habremos sido hechos semejantes a Él. De alguna manera — y este es uno de los grandes misterios de la Escritura — Dios nos hará santos sin borrar quiénes somos. Nos purificará sin eliminarnos. Nuestra identidad, nuestra memoria, nuestra libertad: todo ello llevado a través de una santidad que aún no podemos imaginar. Cómo hará esto es un gran misterio.

blocks.en: This is the shape of the whole discourse. It moves from what we cannot know, the date, through what we are promised, the events of that day, to what we can barely imagine, what we shall become. It begins in humility, moves through hope, and closes in wonder. And chapter 25 turns it all into one urgent call. The ten virgins teach us to be ready, for five had oil and five did not, and the door was shut. The talents teach us to be faithful with whatever we have been given, that we may hear, "Well done, good and faithful servant." And the sheep and the goats show the King judging the nations and saying that whatever was done to the least of His brethren was done to Him. Watch, be faithful, and love — for the King will surely come. As Augustine prayed, "You have made us for Yourself, and our heart is restless until it rests in You." The face-to-face sight of God is the rest toward which every human longing has unknowingly reached, and the final mystery — that God will make us holy without undoing us — is the wonder we carry home.
blocks.es_reference: Esta es la forma de todo el discurso. Se mueve desde lo que no podemos saber, la fecha, a través de lo que se nos promete, los eventos de ese día, hasta lo que apenas podemos imaginar, en qué nos convertiremos. Comienza en la humildad, avanza por la esperanza, y cierra en el asombro. Y el capítulo 25 lo vuelve todo un llamado urgente. Las diez vírgenes nos enseñan a estar preparados, porque cinco tenían aceite y cinco no, y la puerta fue cerrada. Los talentos nos enseñan a ser fieles con lo que se nos ha dado, para que oigamos: "Bien, buen siervo y fiel." Y las ovejas y los cabritos muestran al Rey juzgando a las naciones y diciendo que cuanto se hizo al más pequeño de sus hermanos, a Él se le hizo. Velad, sed fieles, y amad — porque el Rey ciertamente vendrá. Como oró Agustín: "Nos hiciste para ti, y nuestro corazón está inquieto hasta que descanse en ti." La visión de Dios cara a cara es el descanso hacia el cual todo anhelo humano ha alcanzado sin saberlo, y el misterio final — que Dios nos hará santos sin deshacernos — es el asombro que llevamos a casa.

blocks.en: "Beloved, now we are children of God; and it has not yet been revealed what we shall be, but we know that when He is revealed, we shall be like Him, for we shall see Him as He is." — 1 John 3:2 (NKJV)
blocks.es_reference: "Amados, ahora somos hijos de Dios, y aún no se ha manifestado lo que hemos de ser; pero sabemos que cuando él apareciere, seremos semejantes a él, porque le veremos como él es." — 1 Juan 3:2 (RVG)

mc.stem: As Jesus left the temple, He predicted that:
options: Not one stone would be left upon another
mc.why: This was fulfilled in A.D. 70 when the temple was destroyed.

mc.stem: On the Mount of Olives the disciples asked Jesus how many questions?
options: Three — about the temple, His coming, and the end of the age
mc.why: Jesus answered all three, woven so closely that interpreters still debate them.

mc.stem: The temple was destroyed in A.D. 70, which was:
options: About forty years after Jesus' prediction, within a generation
mc.why: That part of Jesus' answer was fulfilled within a single generation.

mc.stem: During the siege, the historian Josephus records that the famine grew so severe that people:
options: Ate shoe leather and even, in one case, turned to cannibalism
mc.why: Social order collapsed as the search for food became the only priority.

mc.stem: Jesus said that the gospel of the kingdom will be preached in all the world, and then:
mc.why: The worldwide witness of the gospel marks the age before the end.

mc.stem: About the exact date of His return, Jesus said:
options: Not even He knew it, but the Father only
It would be in one generation
mc.why: Only the Father knows the day and hour (Matthew 24:36).

mc.stem: By the standard of Deuteronomy 18, a prophet whose prediction fails is:
mc.why: Every date-setter has failed, disqualifying himself by Scripture's own test.

options: It used homemade numerology and harmed those who trusted it
mc.why: People drained savings and abandoned careers; the harm was real and lasting.

mc.stem: Instead of giving a date, Jesus gave parables and images whose point was:
options: Be ready, for you will not see it coming
mc.why: He answered not the question they asked but the one they should have: Are you ready?

mc.stem: In the parable of the ten virgins, the five who were shut out were the ones who:
options: Had no oil ready when the bridegroom came
mc.why: The bridegroom was delayed, and the unprepared found the door shut.

options: He first came as a conquering king, then as a servant
He first came as the suffering Servant, and will return as a conquering King

mc.stem: First Thessalonians 4 assures believers that at Christ's return:

mc.why: Jewish readers heard all three at once when Paul said the trumpet would sound.

options: See Him as He is and be like Him
mc.why: In the Old Testament none could look on God; made like Him, we will see Him face to face.

options: Make us holy without erasing who we are
Keep us exactly as we are now
mc.why: Our identity, memory, and freedom are carried through a holiness we cannot yet imagine.

mc.stem: The discourse and chapter 25 together call the hearer to:
options: Watch, be faithful, and love, for the King will come
mc.why: The ten virgins, the talents, and the sheep and goats press readiness, faithfulness, and love.

sa.prompt: Describe the setting of the Olivet Discourse and the three questions the disciples asked.
sa.model: As Jesus and the disciples were leaving the temple, He said that not one stone would be left upon another. On the Mount of Olives they came to Him with three questions: when would the temple be destroyed, what would be the sign of His coming, and what is the sign of the end of the age. Jesus answered all three, but the answers are woven together so closely that interpreters still debate which verse belongs to which question. This is the great discourse on the last things. It was given less to satisfy our curiosity about the timing than to make His people ready, so we should hold it with humility and let its purpose be preparation rather than speculation.

sa.prompt: How was Jesus' prediction about the temple fulfilled in A.D. 70?
sa.model: The temple fell in A.D. 70, about forty years after Jesus spoke, so that part of His answer was fulfilled within a single generation. The Roman legions under Titus laid siege to the city and cut every supply line, and inside the walls the people were destroyed by famine, civil war, and disease. Josephus records starvation so severe that people ate shoe leather and even turned to cannibalism. The Second Temple was burned to its foundations, and because the gold ornaments had melted, soldiers pried apart the very stones to recover it, literally fulfilling the word that not one stone would be left upon another. Hundreds of thousands died and tens of thousands were enslaved, and for the Jew this was the end of his world, for the priesthood, the sacrifices, and the central place of worship all came to an end.

sa.prompt: What signs of the age did Jesus describe, and what do interpreters disagree about?
sa.model: Jesus described the character of the whole age. There would be false christs who deceive many, wars and rumors of wars, famines and earthquakes, but these are only the beginning of sorrows. His people would be hated and persecuted, yet the gospel of the kingdom would be preached in all the world to every nation, and then the end would come. He spoke of the abomination of desolation and a great tribulation, and finally of the Son of Man coming on the clouds with power and great glory to gather His elect. Interpreters disagree over how much of this language pointed to the fall of Jerusalem in A.D. 70 and how much reaches forward to the final coming, and faithful readers differ. What is certain is the fig tree's lesson, that when these things begin the end is near, and that heaven and earth will pass away but His words will not.

sa.prompt: Why can no one know the date of Christ's return, and what does the failure of date-setters show?
sa.model: Jesus said plainly that not even He knew the date of His return, but the Father only, so no one can calculate it. That has not stopped people from predicting it for two thousand years, and every one has been wrong. By the standard of Deuteronomy 18, a prophet whose prediction fails is a false prophet, so these date-setters disqualified themselves by Scripture's own test. The 2011 prediction of Harold Camping is a modern warning, for he used homemade numerology to convince thousands of a date, then simply moved it when nothing happened, and the harm was real as people drained their savings and abandoned their careers. The failure of every date-setter shows that we are not meant to calculate the day but to be ready, for Jesus answered not the question people asked but the one they should have: are you ready?

sa.prompt: What do the parables and images of readiness (the ten virgins; one taken, one left) teach?
sa.model: Instead of a date, Jesus gave parables and images of readiness. Ten virgins waited for the bridegroom: five had enough oil and five did not, the bridegroom was delayed, and the five who were unprepared found the door shut when he finally came. In other images two are sleeping in a bed, two are working in a field, and two are grinding at the mill, and in each case one is taken and one is left. The circumstances are completely ordinary, with no one in the middle of a dramatic moment; they are simply sleeping, working, and going about their day. The point is unmistakable: they will not see it coming, so they had better always be ready. Jesus refused to answer the timing question and pressed instead the question they should have been asking, which is whether they are prepared and watching.

sa.prompt: Describe the main millennial positions and the even-handed way this unit treats them.
sa.model: Christians who love the same Bible have long held different views of the thousand years of Revelation 20. The premillennial view holds that Christ returns before a coming reign on the earth, the amillennial view understands the thousand years as a picture of Christ's present reign between His two comings, and the postmillennial view expects Christ to return after a long age in which the gospel's influence grows. Sincere, Bible-loving believers have held each of these for centuries, and none of them has ever been a test of Christian fellowship. This unit names the positions fairly without pushing any one of them. On the central things every view agrees: Christ will return bodily and visibly, the dead will be raised, and there will be a final judgment. We do better to stand together on what is certain than to divide over the order of events.

sa.prompt: How does the unit contrast Christ's two comings, and what does 1 Thessalonians 4 promise?
sa.model: The first time Jesus came, He came as the suffering Servant of Isaiah, born in a stable, rejected by His own, and crucified between two thieves, but when He comes again He will come as a conquering King, and the contrast could not be more complete. First Thessalonians 4 gives the clearest picture of that day: the dead in Christ will rise first, then those who are alive will be caught up to join them, all at the sound of the trumpet. The believers in Thessalonica were anxious about loved ones who had died while waiting, and Paul assured them that death is no barrier, for those who died in Christ will not be left behind but will be the first to be raised. So the same Lord who came in lowliness will return in power, and neither the living nor the dead who belong to Him will miss that day.

sa.prompt: How does the unit answer the question of the state of the dead, against 'soul sleep'?
sa.model: Scripture rejects the idea of soul sleep, the notion that the soul is unconscious between death and the resurrection. The Lord told the thief on the cross that he would be with Him in Paradise that very day, and Paul says that to be absent from the body is to be present with the Lord, so the soul remains awake and in communion with God immediately after death. The references to sleep in Scripture are understood as a metaphor for the rest of the physical body in the grave rather than the condition of the soul itself. The body is only the mailbox, and once the letter is posted it is already in the sender's hands even before it reaches its destination; the mailbox may rust and be replaced, but the letter, the real person, is kept safe until the appointed day of delivery, which is the resurrection.

sa.prompt: What will believers become, according to 1 John 3:2, and what mystery does this involve?
sa.model: When we meet the Lord we will receive glorified bodies like His resurrection body, which passed through locked doors, was recognized by His friends and sometimes not, and ate fish not from need but because He could. But something greater awaits, for First John 3:2 says that when He appears we shall see Him as He is and we shall be like Him. In the Old Testament no one could look directly on God, and Moses saw only His back, for the glory would have destroyed sinful men, but on that day we will see Him face to face because we will have been made like Him. This involves a great mystery, that God will make us holy without erasing who we are; He will purify us without deleting us, carrying our identity, our memory, and our freedom through a holiness we cannot yet imagine.

sa.prompt: Describe the arc of the discourse and how chapter 25 turns it into a call to action.
sa.model: The discourse moves from what we cannot know, the date, through what we are promised, the events of that day, to what we can barely imagine, what we shall become; it begins in humility, moves through hope, and closes in wonder. Chapter 25 turns all of this into one urgent call. The ten virgins teach us to be ready, for five had oil and five did not, and the door was shut. The talents teach us to be faithful with whatever we have been given, that we may hear, well done, good and faithful servant. And the sheep and the goats show the King judging the nations and saying that whatever was done to the least of His brethren was done to Him. So the proper response to the last things is to watch, to be faithful, and to love, for the King will surely come, and the final wonder is that God will make us holy without undoing us.
